596.title: Svayamprabha's welcome
596.hook: lost and thirsty in the dark, then a golden city and a welcome
596.carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god
596.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes a guest is offered water on arrival and fed before any business, and families often quote atithi devo bhava for it. Svayamprabha is remembered as one of the Ramayana's ascetic women, alongside Shabari.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's ring went south with Hanuman, and three parties came home empty. Nama: the name carries the one it names.
screen: `NAMA: THE NAME CARRIES THE ONE IT NAMES.`

segments.voice: The southern party is having a terrible time. They've searched the Vindhya hills, forest after forest, cave after cave. Nothing. Now they're lost, hungry and desperately thirsty, in dry country with no stream in sight, and the month is running out. Then they see birds flying out of a hole in the hillside: cranes, geese, waterbirds, their wings wet. Where there are wet birds, there's water somewhere. So in they go.
screen: `LOST IN THE VINDHYA HILLS.` → `THIRSTY.` → `WET BIRDS FROM A HOLE.`

segments.voice: The cave is dark and overgrown with creepers. Valmiki calls it Rikshabila, the bear's hole. Hanuman goes first. The monkeys hold on to one another in the pitch black and go deeper, with no idea what's at the end. And then light. A place that shouldn't exist underground: golden trees glowing like fire, palaces of gold and silver, lotus pools, heaps of fruit and honey. In the middle sits a woman ascetic, dressed in bark and black antelope skin, shining with her own light. Hanuman approaches with joined palms: whose place is this? It was built by Maya, she says, the great architect of the demons. He lived here with Hema, a celestial dancer, until Indra killed him. I am Svayamprabha, daughter of Merusavarni, and I keep it for my friend. Then comes what she does next. She doesn't question them or test them. Eat first, she says. Drink. Rest. Then tell me your story. That order is an old Hindu teaching. The Taittiriya Upanishad sends students home from their teacher with a few lines to live by, and one of them is atithi devo bhava: let the guest be a god to you. A guest arrives, and you treat them the way you'd treat the divine at your door: water, a seat, food, before any questions. Svayamprabha doesn't know these monkeys. They could be anyone. She feeds them anyway. That's why, in so many Hindu homes, you can't get through the door without someone handing you water and a plate before you've even sat down.
screen: `INTO THE BEAR'S HOLE.` · `A GOLDEN CITY BUILT BY MAYA.` · `EAT FIRST, THEN TALK.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, take one slow sip; if not, just notice your mouth and throat. Breathe in and remember the parched monkeys following wet wings into the dark; breathe out and feel what it is to be fed before anyone asks who you are. Then think of one person who'll come through your door, or to your desk, this week, and decide what you'll offer them first: water, tea, a seat. That's atithi devo bhava, the way Hindu homes live it.
Svayamprabha, 'self-shining': the ascetic who keeps a golden city hidden in a cave, and feeds the lost monkeys before asking who they are.
Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is god. Svayamprabha fed them before she asked their names. Until tomorrow.

597.title: Svayamprabha asks nothing
597.hook: cover your eyes, you're out, and she asks nothing back
597.carry: sattvic dana: a gift that asks nothing back
597.howItsDone: Many Hindu families give dana quietly, without their names. Some later tellings, such as the Adhyatma Ramayana, have Svayamprabha go on to meet Rama; in Valmiki she simply goes back into her cave.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a golden city underground, and Svayamprabha's welcome. Atithi devo bhava, the guest is god.

Fed and rested, the monkeys tell Svayamprabha everything: Rama, Sita, Ravana, the search, Sugriva's deadline. She listens. And then Hanuman asks the question that's been sitting under all that good food. How do we get out? They came in by holding each other in the dark, through a long, twisting passage. It's not easy to leave this place alive, Svayamprabha tells them. Not without help. Then she says she'll help.
screen: `THEY TELL HER EVERYTHING.` → `HOW DO WE GET OUT?` → `NOT WITHOUT HELP.`

segments.voice: Svayamprabha says she'll bring them out by the power of her austerities. Close your eyes, she says. Cover them with your hands. They do. And in an instant they're outside, standing near the shore, with the great southern ocean roaring in front of them. She shows them where they are, wishes them well, and goes back into her cave. Then the cruel part. Inside the cave it didn't feel long. But outside the trees are in flower, and when Angada counts the days, the month Sugriva gave them is gone, and they still have nothing to report. Now look at what Svayamprabha asks in return. Nothing. In a book full of bargains, a pact for a pact, an army for a kingdom, she gives food, rest and rescue, and walks back into the dark. Hindus have a word for giving: dana. And the Bhagavad Gita sorts gifts by kind. The highest, the sattvic gift, the pure one, is given simply because it ought to be given, at the right time and place, to someone who can do nothing for you in return. Svayamprabha's gift fits exactly. The monkeys can't repay her, and she doesn't ask. That's why many Hindu families give quietly: a donation with no name on it, food sent to the temple kitchen, what Hindi speakers call gupt daan, secret giving. The giving is the point, not the thanks. And now, on the shore, with the sea in front of them and the deadline behind them, the southern party has a new problem.
screen: `CLOSE YOUR EYES. OUT BY THE SEA.` · `THE MONTH IS GONE. SHE ASKS NOTHING.` · `SATTVIC DANA: A GIFT THAT ASKS NOTHING BACK.` · `GUPT DAAN: SECRET GIVING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or cover them gently with your palms, the way the monkeys did. Breathe in and remember a time someone helped you and asked nothing back. Breathe out and choose one small gift you can give today with no name on it: a donation, a meal, a favor nobody will hear about. If you pray, offer it quietly to God; if you don't, just let it go out without waiting for thanks.
Svayamprabha, who leads the monkeys out of her cave by her own power. Eyes covered, and they're out by the southern sea, but the month is already gone.
Your line: sattvic dana, a gift that asks nothing back. Svayamprabha walked back into her cave. That's day five hundred ninety-seven.

598.title: Sitting down on the shore
598.hook: late, empty-handed, and tempted to hide or give up
598.howItsDone: Prayopavesha, fasting unto death, appears in the epics as a solemn vow; Hindu teachers today speak of it only in very specific traditional contexts, and in the Ramayana the monkeys' vow is interrupted before it's carried out.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Svayamprabha led them out with eyes covered, a sattvic gift that asked nothing back. But the month was already gone.

On the beach, Angada does the math, and it's bad. They're late. They haven't found Sita. Sugriva warned that anyone who came back late would answer with their life. And Angada carries a private fear on top of that. He's Vali's son. His uncle took his father's throne with Rama's help. Angada wonders whether Sugriva has ever really trusted him. Back late and empty-handed? He decides he isn't going back at all.
screen: `ANGADA DOES THE MATH.` → `A PRIVATE FEAR.` → `HE WON'T GO BACK.`

segments.voice: Despair spreads fast. Angada tells the others he'll fast to death right here on the shore, a vow called prayopavesha. One monkey, named Tara, a different Tara from Vali's widow, offers another way out: let's go back to the cave. It has food, water, safety, and no one could reach us. Several monkeys like the idea. Then Hanuman speaks. To Angada he's gentle: Sugriva is fair, and you're dear to him; don't assume the worst. About the cave he's blunt: Lakshmana's arrows could split that cave open. Hiding isn't safety. And quietly he wins the others over, one by one. Angada isn't convinced. He spreads sacred darbha grass on the shore and sits down, and the others sit with him, a long line along the sea, talking about Rama and Sita, and about Jatayu, the old vulture who died fighting Ravana. Hindus know this posture. The Bhagavad Gita opens with it: the warrior Arjuna, facing a duty he can't bear, drops his bow and sinks down in his chariot. Krishna's first answer, more or less, is: stand up. The teaching under both scenes is dharma, your rightful duty, the part that's yours to do. Being late doesn't cancel it. Being afraid doesn't cancel it. Despair says sit down and disappear; dharma says go back, tell the truth, and keep going. And up on the hillside behind them, out of a cave, something very old is listening.
screen: `PRAYOPAVESHA: A FAST TO DEATH.` · `HANUMAN: HIDING ISN'T SAFETY.` · `ARJUNA SAT DOWN TOO.` · `DESPAIR DOESN'T CANCEL YOUR DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Notice, gently, whether there's somewhere in your life you've quietly sat down and given up, not to fix it now, just to see it. Breathe in and name it; breathe out and ask what your part there still is, one small next step: a call, an apology, showing up late instead of never. If you pray, many Hindus call on Hanuman when they're afraid; you can too. If giving up ever feels like more than that, please reach out today: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
Prayopavesha, sitting down to fast unto death: the vow Angada takes today on the shore, when Hanuman argues that hiding in the cave isn't safety either.
Your line: despair doesn't cancel your dharma. Even here, the story isn't over. See you tomorrow.

599.title: Who speaks of my brother?
599.hook: a hungry old vulture hears his brother's name
599.carry: tarpana: water poured, a loved one named
599.howItsDone: Tarpana is offered in the shraddha rites after a death and every year in Pitru Paksha, often with sesame seeds in the water, naming the departed and, commonly, three generations of ancestors. Storytellers often pair Sampati and Jatayu as two brothers who both serve Rama.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Angada sat down on the shore to give up, and we learned that despair doesn't cancel your dharma. While they sat, the monkeys talked about Jatayu.

Out of a cave on the hillside comes an enormous old bird. What's left of his wings is burned. He drags himself onto the rocks and looks down at a beach covered with monkeys, all sitting perfectly still. And he says to himself, more or less: what luck. A meal, lined up and waiting to die. As each one goes, I'll eat him. The monkeys hear him. Nobody on that beach is sitting quite so still anymore.
screen: `AN OLD BIRD ON THE ROCKS.` → `BURNED WINGS.` → `WHAT LUCK: A MEAL.`

segments.voice: The monkeys are terrified. Angada, already in despair, says it aloud: death has come for us in the shape of a bird. Even Jatayu gave his life for Rama, he says. We're dying for Rama too. The old bird freezes. Who is speaking of my brother? he calls down. I haven't heard that name in so long. Is Jatayu dead? The hunter has become a mourner. His name is Sampati, and Jatayu was his younger brother. The monkeys, still uneasy, help him down, and Angada tells him everything: Sita taken, Jatayu's fight with Ravana in the sky, and his death. Sampati grieves right there on the beach. And in Valmiki's telling, he asks the monkeys to carry him to the edge of the sea, so he can offer water to his brother. They carry him down, and the old bird pours water for Jatayu. This is one of the oldest things Hindus do for their dead. It's called tarpana. You pour water from cupped hands, often with sesame seeds in it, and you say the person's name, and the names of your parents and grandparents before them. Families do it in the shraddha rites after a death, and every year in Pitru Paksha, the fortnight for the ancestors. The teaching under it: the people we lose aren't simply gone. They're named, fed and remembered, and the bond keeps running. Jatayu's death looked like a defeat months ago in the story. Now his name, said out loud on a beach, saves the whole southern party.
screen: `ANGADA NAMES JATAYU.` · `SAMPATI, JATAYU'S BROTHER.` · `TARPANA: WATER POURED, A LOVED ONE NAMED.` · `NAMED, FED, REMEMBERED.`

If no one comes to mind, think of someone who carries a loss, and hold them instead.

600.title: Wings over his brother
600.hook: two young brothers race toward the sun
600.howItsDone: Storytellers often pair Sampati's sacrifice for Jatayu with Jatayu's sacrifice for Sita: two brothers, each burned or wounded for someone else.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sampati heard his brother's name and poured water for him by the sea. Tarpana, water poured, a loved one named.

Two brothers race straight up toward the sun. It's day six hundred, and Sampati is telling the monkeys how it began. When Jatayu and I were young, he says, we were proud of our flying. We were rivals the way brothers are, each sure he was the stronger. So one day we raced. It's an old kind of contest: two brothers, each needing to win, neither willing to turn back first.
screen: `A RACE TOWARD THE SUN.` → `DAY SIX HUNDRED.` → `TWO PROUD YOUNG BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: They climbed until the earth below looked small. Then the heat came. Jatayu, the younger, began to faint, and Sampati spread his own wings over his brother to shade him. His wings burned. He fell, landed here on the Vindhya hills, and has lived without wings ever since. Many teachers read that race as ahankara, the Hindu word for ego, literally the I-maker: the part of you that has to be the biggest, the fastest, the first. The Bhagavad Gita lists it among the things a wise person lets go of. Notice what ahankara did: it sent two brothers straight at the sun. And notice what the story remembers. Not who flew higher, but the moment Sampati stopped racing and covered his brother. The race was for the I; the burn was for love. Then he waited, a long time. A sage named Nishakara comforted him and told him that one day Rama's messengers would come searching for Sita, and if Sampati helped them, his wings would grow back. Without wings he couldn't hunt, so his son Suparshva brought him food. One day Suparshva came back late and empty-handed. He had seen a dark giant flying over the sea carrying a weeping woman. That was Ravana, Sampati tells the monkeys. That was your Sita. And the monkeys, who sat down to die an hour ago, sit up straight.
screen: `SAMPATI SHADES HIS BROTHER.` · `THE WINGS BURN.` · `AHANKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · `SUPARSHVA SAW RAVANA.`

segments.voice: Let your arms rest open a little, like folded wings. Think of somewhere you're racing someone right now: for a grade, for credit, for the last word. Breathe in and notice the I that needs to win; Hindus call it ahankara. Breathe out and picture spreading a wing over the person you're racing instead. You don't have to lose. Just notice which moment you'd want remembered.
Sampati. He lost his wings shading his brother from the sun, and waited, wingless, for Rama's messengers.
Your line: ahankara races, love shields. Six hundred days of showing up. See you tomorrow.

601.title: Sampati sees Lanka
601.hook: a vulture's sight reaches Lanka, and his wings grow back
601.howItsDone: The Kishkindha Kanda closes on the shore with the question of who can cross the sea; in recitations, Sampati's vision is the turning point that sends listeners into the Sundara Kanda, which some families recite on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sampati raced his brother toward the sun, then burned his wings to shade him. Ahankara races, love shields.

Where is she? That's the only question that matters now, and Sampati can answer it. Vultures, he tells the monkeys, see very far. We're born with it. Our food is far below us, so our eyes reach far. From this hill I can see a hundred yojanas, across the whole sea. The monkeys turn and look where he's looking. All they can see is water.
screen: `WHERE IS SHE?` → `A VULTURE'S SIGHT.` → `A HUNDRED YOJANAS.`

segments.voice: Sampati looks south and tells them what he sees. An island, a hundred yojanas away. On it, Lanka, a golden city built by Vishvakarma, the architect of the gods. And in it, kept in Ravana's inner grounds and guarded by rakshasa women, is Sita, dressed in yellow silk, grieving. The answer doesn't come from the armies or the kings. It comes from an old, wingless bird who an hour ago wanted to eat them. Then the old promise comes true. Because Sampati has helped Rama's messengers, his wings begin to grow, right there in front of them. He feels young and strong again, and he tells them: make the effort. Cross the sea. Then he spreads his new wings and flies off to see whether he can still fly. Hindus have a word for what Sampati just did: seva, service. Not a job, not a favor traded, but help given to God's work as a kind of worship. It's why families cook in temple kitchens, sweep the hall before a festival, and serve food at a wedding without being asked. In bhakti, the devotional heart of Hinduism, seva is worship you do with your hands. Many teachers read Sampati's wings this way: he gave the one thing he had left, his eyes, to Rama's cause, and the giving made him whole. Now the monkeys know where Sita is. Between them and her lies a hundred yojanas of open sea, and one question left: who can cross it?
screen: `SITA IN LANKA, ACROSS THE SEA.` · `SAMPATI'S WINGS GROW BACK.` · `SEVA: SERVICE AS WORSHIP.` · `THE GIVING MADE HIM WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Let your gaze go as far as it can, out a window or to the farthest wall, the way Sampati looked across the sea. Breathe in and let your sight be wide. Then bring it close: what's one small seva within reach today? Washing up after someone else's meal, helping set up at a temple or a community event, carrying something for someone. If you pray, offer it to God as you do it; if not, just do it fully, as a gift.
Sampati. With a vulture's sight he sees Sita in Lanka, a hundred yojanas over the sea, and his wings grow back.
Your line: seva, service offered as worship. Sampati gave what he had, and his wings came back. Tomorrow, who can make the jump? That's day six hundred one.

602.title: How far can you jump?
602.hook: a hundred yojanas of water, and a circle of monkeys saying out loud how far each of them can jump
602.carry: satya: say what you can really do
602.howItsDone: Readers of the Kishkindha Kanda often linger on this scene of the monkeys stating their limits on the shore, because it sets up the moment when Jambavan turns to Hanuman.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sampati's wings grew back as he told the monkeys where Sita was. Seva heals the one who serves.

The job is finally clear, and it's impossible. Sita is in Lanka, an island a hundred yojanas across the ocean. A yojana is an old measure of distance, many miles long. The monkeys walk down to the shore and look at the water. Valmiki describes it like something alive: huge waves, sea creatures, a roar that never stops. The whole army sits down on the sand, quiet. Nobody wants to say the obvious thing first.
screen: `THE JOB IS CLEAR.` → `A HUNDRED YOJANAS OF SEA.` → `THE ARMY SITS DOWN, QUIET.`

segments.voice: Angada, the young prince who leads them, breaks the silence: who here can cross this? One by one, the monkeys answer honestly. One says he can leap ten yojanas. Another, twenty. Another, thirty. On it goes, each a little further, up to the old bear Jambavan, who says ninety. When he was young, he adds, he could have done it easily. He once circled the great god Vishnu when Vishnu strode across the worlds in three steps. But age has taken that. Then Angada speaks. He thinks he can jump the full hundred. What he isn't sure of is the jump back. Jambavan answers kindly but firmly. You're the leader, the root of the whole expedition. You don't send the root. Nobody brags here, and nobody pretends. That's a Hindu virtue with a name: satya, truthfulness. In yoga it's one of the yamas, the first restraints a student is asked to keep. And satya isn't only about not lying to others. It's not lying about yourself: not puffing up your number, and not shrinking it either. Every monkey on that beach tells the truth, the numbers fall short, and that's allowed. Honest limits are how the right one gets found. This week: a guest fed like a god, a gift that asked nothing, despair on the shore, water for a brother, ego and love, seva, and now satya. One monkey hasn't spoken. He's sitting apart, saying nothing at all.
screen: `WHO CAN CROSS THIS?` · `TEN, TWENTY, THIRTY... NINETY.` · `ANGADA: I'M NOT SURE OF THE WAY BACK.` · then, large: `SATYA: THE HONEST NUMBER.` · then: `ONE MONKEY HASN'T SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that feels too far to cross: a task, a conversation, a long recovery. Instead of measuring the whole distance, ask honestly how far you can go today, ten yojanas or twenty, and hold that number without shame and without puffing it up. That's satya, turned toward yourself. With each breath out, let the gap between what you can do and what is needed simply be true, for now.
Yojana, an old measure of distance many miles long: what the monkeys count in as each says how far he can jump, and the numbers fall short of a hundred.
Your line: satya, say what you can really do. Not a hundred yet, anyway. Day six hundred two, done.
